title: Two teachers
hookLine: he masters the deep states taught by Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta, and leaves: good, but not the end (MN 26)
last: BIMBISARA — A PROMISE TO COME BACK.

cards: What comes after getting good at something? Years on a language, an instrument, a craft, and people start coming to you for advice. Then, right at the top of it, a quiet question can show up anyway: is this it?
Not because the thing is bad. Because it isn't what you came for.
The wanderer left the palace to find an answer to age, sickness and death, and in his world there are teachers of meditation with communities of students around them. He goes to the first.

teach.b: This story comes from the Buddha himself, in a sutta where he looks back on his search.
His first teacher was Alara Kalama, who taught a meditation leading to a very deep state called the base of nothingness: a mind so still it rests in nothing at all.
The wanderer learned it fast, and soon could reach it himself. Alara was delighted, and did something generous. You know what I know, he said.
Let's lead this community together, as equals. The wanderer thought about it and said no. This teaching, he says, doesn't lead to the end of suffering, only to that state.
When you come out of it, you're still you, with everything you carried in.

So he went to a second teacher, Uddaka Ramaputta, whose father had taught an even subtler state: neither perception nor non-perception, a stillness so fine it can barely be described. Again he mastered it.
Again he was offered leadership, this time of the whole community. Again he said no, and walked away. Notice what he doesn't say.

teach.h: NOT FRAUDS. JUST NOT THE END.
teach.b: He doesn't call these teachers frauds or these states useless. Buddhists still teach these deep meditative states today, and later suttas list them among the attainments of meditation.

What he says is simpler: good, but not the end. That's this week, the going forth, in one line: samvega, the doorway, the midnight ride, the cut hair, a horse's grief, Bimbisara's offer, and two teachers.
Each time, something good is left behind, because it isn't the end.

how: Buddhist meditators still study the deep absorptions and formless states, and teachers often tell the story of the two teachers to show that calm states, however deep, are a means rather than the goal.

o: two rival kings who fought over Magadha
two monks who shaved his head at the river
the masters whose deep states he learned and left

games.q: who taught what — tap the pairs.
p: said: good, but not the end

s: the Buddha called his first teachers frauds
he mastered what they taught and left because it didn't end suffering, not because it was false.
Alara Kalama offered to lead his community together with the wanderer
the story of the two teachers is told by the Buddha himself in a sutta
in MN 26, looking back on his search.

games.q: your teacher says: you know everything I know. lead this community with me. what do you do?
o: accept, and teach the base of nothingness.
decline, because it doesn't end suffering.
games.why: he declines, twice, to two teachers. the states were real and deep, but they didn't end suffering.

practice: Think of one thing you've learned well, a skill, a subject, a habit, a practice, and give it its due for a breath or two: the hours it took, the work it was.

Then ask it gently, what's next, not to throw it away, just to see if there's a further step, a deeper question, something it points toward. Let the question sit beside the skill without rushing for an answer.

wordCard.voice: Two teachers. Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta, who taught the wanderer deep meditative states, and whom he left because the states were good, but not the end.

orig.note: Pali: the base of nothingness, the deep state Alara Kalama taught.

carryVoice: Your line: good, but not the end. Two masters, two kind offers, two quiet refusals. A week of leaving, finished.

sources.ref: Ariyapariyesana Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 26): the two teachers
